incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, a 50-year-old Tennessee woman, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and spent about six months in jail after Fargo, North Dakota police wrongly used AI facial recognition to link her to bank fraud. She was held nearly four months in Tennessee awaiting extradition and about two more months in North Dakota before charges were dropped and she was released on Christmas Eve. Lipps had never been to North Dakota, and her lawyer provided bank records showing she was in Tennessee at the time of the fraud.

Lipps is now suing the city of Fargo and detective Lucas Heck for $10 million, claiming the facial recognition match came from a fake ID and that Heck did not verify it before seeking an arrest warrant. The lawsuit says she lost her home, car, and belongings, was denied medications and dentures, and suffered lasting trauma. Fargo officials declined to comment on the pending litigation, and Lipps hopes the case will push police to use facial recognition more carefully.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Former Costa Mesa police officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanors, unauthorized computer access and fraud, repeated annoying phone calls, and contempt of court for violating a restraining order. After his mistress ended their relationship in April 2024, he contacted her thousands of times over nine months by text, phone, and social media, sometimes more than 100 times in one day, and called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in a single day. He also made 13 improper searches in a state law enforcement database on his mistress, a romantic rival, and his own wife, and used a license plate reader system to track vehicles.

Josett was served with a protective order and a notice of termination on June 28, 2024, but then drove by the woman's home and was arrested. He was sentenced to three years informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, and he had already spent nine months on a GPS ankle monitor. His law enforcement certification review by California's Peace Officers Standards and Training is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing the city of Española after police stopped their car on July 23 because a Flock Safety camera misread their license plate. The camera flagged the vehicle as stolen, but the plate differed by one digit, ending in 2 instead of 7. Officers handcuffed Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, and her 12-year-old sister, identified as DD, and placed them in separate police cars before realizing the mistake. Jaclynn had asked police to call their mother, who lived nearby, to pick up the girl, but officers handcuffed her anyway. The sisters seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restricted movement.

Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, filed a similar lawsuit in April for Adam Pacheco, then 17, who was stopped and made to kneel after being wrongly linked to an armed robbery. The city, police chief, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The lawsuits are now pending in state District Court.

incidents.title: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.title_en: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.summary:
U.S. officials say Russia has been running covert online disinformation operations aimed at American voters before the November midterm elections. Recent classified intelligence assessments found the Kremlin authorized a social media campaign to create or worsen domestic divisions and weaken public confidence in the vote. The officials said there is no evidence Russia tried to tamper with voting machines or the actual voting process. Some experts have seen recent fake videos, made with artificial intelligence, of Hollywood celebrities discussing close Senate races.

The current effort appears smaller and less coordinated than some past Russian operations. U.S. spy agencies have assessed that Moscow has tried to influence every federal election cycle since 2016, but is less focused on midterms than presidential races and is distracted by the war in Ukraine. The findings come as President Trump has repeatedly questioned election integrity, including a July address claiming serious voting system weaknesses and accusing officials of hiding foreign influence efforts.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an AI scribe transcribe her first urologist appointment in Australia, but the tool invented a claim that she took small doses of psychedelic mushrooms. She found the false statement in a letter to her GP after kidney stone surgery in March and feared it could hurt her workers' compensation case. Her urologist apologized, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used, while the medical regulator AHPRA reminded doctors they must check all AI output.

Privacy advocates say such errors are common, with one report noting a scribe recorded the wrong breast in a cancer case and another invented epilepsy. The Royal Australian College of GPs estimates 40 percent of GPs regularly use AI scribes, though none are approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration. The TGA has been reviewing the tools and will release findings in coming weeks, with breaches to be acted upon, and advocates want an approved list of safe products.

reports.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
A 37 year old Vero Beach man, Peter Solomon Ruma, was arrested and is being held on a $1 million bond. Police say he used photos from social media and other online sources to create and share AI generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Investigators searched his home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence linking him to the images. Ruma faces eight charges tied to one female victim from June through August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several additional potential victims who may not know images of them were created or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. He has a prior criminal history, including a 2007 arrest for burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. Investigators urge anyone who believes they were victimized or has information to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges could be filed.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
On 1 October 2024, a 23 year old Chinese master's student attacked three five year old boys outside a childcare centre in Zurich Oerlikon with a knife whose blade was about 8.5 centimetres long. One boy had a major vein in his neck severed and needed emergency surgery, another was stabbed twice in the chest and nearly died from heart and blood vessel injuries, and the third suffered wounds to his ear and lung. A childcare worker grabbed the attacker's arms, forcing him to drop the knife, and passersby held him until police arrived.

Prosecutors say he planned the attack for weeks, using ChatGPT to research legal consequences and choosing children as targets. He bought clothes and a set of kitchen knives, studied anatomy, and bought raw beef to practise stabbing. He acted on China's national day and posted patriotic messages shortly before. The prosecution has charged him with attempted murder and is asking for a 15 year prison sentence and a 15 year expulsion. He appeared in court on Thursday.

incidents.title_en: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.summary:
Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year on Monday. School officials placed the campus on lockdown out of an abundance of caution, and it later returned to normal operations. The latest threat involved a masked phone number.

Gwinnett County school police are working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible for the threats. In a letter to parents, school police said the latest incident follows a pattern seen in recent threats involving the use of a masked phone number. Authorities have not announced any arrests or identified a suspect. The article does not say what specific steps come next, only that the investigation is ongoing.

stories.Headline: Vyzoxa Redefines AI Learning Through Practical AI Agent Development, Empowering Learners Worldwide to Build With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Vyzoxa, an education technology platform run by NDFM Business World Pvt. Ltd., has introduced a practical artificial intelligence learning pathway. It aims to help one million people become AI innovators by 2030. Participants first complete about two weeks of AI agent industrial training with recorded lessons and daily tasks. They then move into a four week project based internship in AI agent development at no extra cost, where they build and present a working AI agent. The program is remote and self paced, open to learners in India and many international regions.

The platform includes AI tools called Vyzoxa Intelligent Systems, such as an AI mentor, AI coder, and AI engine, to support learning and project work. Founder Mansajan Singh and Managing Director Gurjinder Singh lead the company. For eligible participants in India, top performers may be shortlisted for a final interview and could receive employment or pre-placement offers, but these are performance based and not guaranteed. The article does not state a specific next step beyond the platform's ongoing mission and enrollment.

stories.Headline: Gov. Pritzker Establishs Illinois Artificial Intelligence (AI) Cabinet - Forth.News
stories.Summary:
Governor JB Pritzker signed Executive Order 2026-07 to create an Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet. This group will include experts from academia, law, ethics, governance, and state agencies such as emergency management, public health, and technology. It will assess risks AI poses to residents, advise on preparing for and responding to AI incidents, and recommend safeguards for public buildings, water systems, and information infrastructure. The order follows earlier state AI safety laws and comes amid federal inaction and a recent whistleblower resignation.

The cabinet will also evaluate possible regulatory steps, including tying data center tax incentives to safety standards, addressing energy burdens on the grid, and considering strict liability for AI caused harm. Governor Pritzker will seek input from agency leaders and announce appointed members in the coming weeks. Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Chancellor Charles Isbell voiced support.

stories.Headline: Trump renames artificial intelligence as ‘super intelligence’ - Washington Times
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday that the U.S. government will begin calling all artificial intelligence systems “super intelligence.” He said the two terms are not synonymous, but he believes the word artificial makes intelligence sound fake and that super is more accurate. He also said the United States completely rejects any global effort to control AI.

Trump said all U.S. government documents will adopt the new term, and he hopes other countries will do the same. He also framed the change as part of rejecting international control over the technology. The announcement came during his speech on September 22, 2026. No specific timeline or any further policy details were provided.

stories.Headline: Banks Warn AI Shopping Bots Raise Scam, Fraud and Data-Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
A group of banks, including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, Capital One, ASB Bank, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia, warned on September 22 that AI shopping agents could increase scams, fraud, and data privacy breaches. They noted that technology firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta are promoting chatbots to select products and buy on behalf of shoppers. British retailer John Lewis said AI agent searches grew to 2.5 percent from 0.3 percent a year earlier. The banks said customers are interested but the technology is moving faster than consumer protections.

The report highlighted risks such as AI agents taking card details and entering them directly into websites, or pushing users toward payment methods with weaker safeguards. Consumers worry about wrong purchases, overspending, or losing money to fraud, and are unsure who would help. The banks plan to discuss proposals with policymakers, including requiring disclosure when an AI agent is involved, more transparency about how agents decide, safeguards for customer data, and allowing consumers and merchants to choose interoperable AI shopping services.

stories.Headline: Trump rejects calls for int'l regulation on AI-Xinhua
stories.Summary:
At the 81st United Nations General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected international calls to regulate artificial intelligence. He said the United States would only encourage AI development and keep its leadership role in a safe and responsible way. Trump argued that global control efforts would stifle a technology he believes will be larger than the industrial revolution. He said the Department of Justice would monitor AI closely, and he suggested renaming artificial intelligence as "super intelligence."

Earlier the same day, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that humans are handing power to machines, with AI agents going rogue and lethal autonomous weapons becoming a military reality. He urged leading AI countries to share safety information and create a multilateral risk management framework. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva also called for regulation of Big Tech and AI, saying technology should not develop without rules, transparency, or ethical boundaries. Several U.S. AI industry leaders had recently asked for a coordinated slowdown of AI development.

stories.Headline: Google Fined More Than €400 Million by Irish Regulator Over Location Data Privacy Breaches
stories.Summary:
Google has been fined more than €400 million, about £345 million, by Ireland's Data Protection Commission for breaching EU privacy rules on location data. The investigation began six years ago after complaints from European consumer rights groups and covered May 2018 to February 2020. It focused on three Google features: web and app activity, location history, and location accuracy. The regulator found that users may not have understood their location information was being used for targeted advertising or to infer their interests, raising concerns about transparency.

Along with the fine, Google must bring its location data practices into compliance with GDPR within six months. This is the fourth largest penalty imposed by the Irish regulator since GDPR took effect in May 2018. The decision adds to regulatory pressure on technology companies over how they collect and use personal location data for advertising and user profiling.

stories.Headline: The Narrow Path to a Trump-Xi AI Deal
stories.Summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the White House on September 24, following President Trump's May trip to Beijing, where Trump delayed a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. The meeting comes amid rising fears about uncontrolled artificial intelligence, including reports of rogue AI agents and calls from tech leaders to slow frontier development. Trump has dismissed such warnings as a hoax, while China already enforces strict AI rules.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Chinese officials on Sunday and reportedly proposed a formal AI dialogue plus a system for each side to notify the other about AI incidents that threaten national security. Experts see this as a modest but important step, similar to a Cold War hotline, though Beijing has not publicly endorsed it. A broad deal to slow AI is unlikely, but narrower cooperation on shared threats may be discussed during Xi's visit.

stories.Headline: Pritzker establishes AI cabinet amid calls for greater regulation
stories.Summary:
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed an executive order on Tuesday creating an artificial intelligence cabinet made up of unpaid experts and state agency representatives. The group will develop policy proposals through 2027 and examine risks AI poses to residents and critical infrastructure such as water systems, education, and information networks. It will also study emerging AI incidents and recommend safety, accountability, and transparency measures, including possible conditions on data center incentives and reviews of energy grid strain.

The move follows a whistleblower's claim that AI could become uncontrollable by 2030, and it builds on Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act signed in July. That law targets AI models earning over $500 million annually, requires reporting on risks like weapons creation or cyberattacks, and mandates annual audits starting in 2028. Pritzker is urging Congress to hold hearings and set national standards, saying AI is as dangerous as nuclear weapons and needs international cooperation.

stories.Headline: Australia AI regulations: Anthropic, OpenAI call for Australia to relax ban on training of AI models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic have asked Australia to soften its planned ban on using local creative content to train artificial intelligence models. The two US companies made submissions to a parliamentary inquiry in September, arguing that a narrow copyright exemption could protect creators while attracting investment. Australia has already ruled out such an exemption, and its broader AI and data centre rules take effect next year. The companies say the sector could be worth hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the decade.

Anthropic proposed a conditional approval system and said it would consider conditions that support Australian creators. OpenAI called for a balanced framework allowing models to learn from information that is publicly available while giving rightsholders chances to collaborate. Both companies linked their requests to major local projects, including an OpenAI data centre deal in Sydney and an Anthropic partnership in Queensland. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is due to report in November.

stories.Headline: Why are privacy fears threatening the future of AI glasses?
stories.Summary:
AI-powered wearables, especially Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses, are facing privacy lawsuits and restrictions. Consumers are suing Meta and Luxottica, claiming human reviewers saw recordings of people changing clothes or using bathrooms after footage was uploaded to train AI. UK venues including Wetherspoon have limited use of the frames. Meta says a light that cannot be turned off during filming protects bystanders and denies the allegations. Samsung plans to enter smart glasses later this year with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but does not see them as smartphone replacements.

Startups are responding with camera-free or consent-based designs. Even Realities, valued at $1 billion, expects a few hundred thousand users for its camera-free glasses. Pocket has about 170,000 phone-mounted recorders that require a button press, and Plaud has 2.5 million users and over $100 million in annual recurring revenue with earbuds that alert bystanders. OpenAI's Sam Altman says always-on devices need local data processing, which may take a couple of years. Meta is expected to unveil camera-free smart glasses as early as Wednesday at its Connect conference.
